articles.title: Greek shipowners put Brussels on the spot over IMO deadlock
articles.summary: Greek shipowners have launched a fresh attack on Brussels ahead of the next round of international shipping emissions negotiations, accusing the European Union of putting its own regulatory interests ahead of a global agreement. Union of Greek Shipowners president Melina Travlos warned on Monday that the EU’s...
articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Regulatory Greek shipowners put Brussels on the spot over IMO deadlock Adis Ajdin November 17, 2026 0 0 1 minute read UGS UGS Greek shipowners have launched a fresh attack on Brussels ahead of the next round of international shipping emissions negotiations, accusing the European Union of putting its own regulatory interests ahead of a global agreement. Union of Greek Shipowners president Melina Travlos warned on Monday that the EU’s unwillingness to compromise risks pushing the International Maritime Organization into another deadlock when talks resume in London next week. Travlos said there had been no meaningful progress since the previous negotiating round in September and questioned whether Brussels was more interested in preserving its regional carbon regulations and the revenue they generate than securing a worldwide deal. Greece and three other EU member states, together controlling around 70% of Europe’s shipping fleet according to Travlos, have repeatedly called for greater flexibility in the European negotiating position. Those appeals, she said, had gone unanswered. The intervention comes ahead of a November 23–27 IMO working group meeting, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session has been scheduled provisionally for December 4, subject to confirmation. The talks will revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism. The negotiations have been held up by disagreements over the design, cost and implementation of the measures. Travlos called for a framework reflecting the availability and cost of alternative fuels, the readiness of supporting infrastructure and competition for new fuels from other industries. She also argued that energy-efficiency improvements and operational measures must remain part of the emissions-reduction toolkit rather than placing almost all the emphasis on alternative fuels. Greek owners have long favoured a single international regulatory regime over overlapping regional requirements. The latest statement sharpens that position by directly questioning the EU’s negotiating intentions just days before governments return to London. articles.title: Container freight rates remain under pressure as major benchmarks decline
articles.summary: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly assessments, with Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) and three major Chinese freight benchmarks declining, while the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded a modest increase. Drewry’s WCI fell 2% to US$4,305 per 40-foot container in its 12...
articles.body: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly assessments, with Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) and three major Chinese freight benchmarks declining, while the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded a modest increase. Drewry’s WCI fell 2% to US$4,305 per 40-foot container in its 12 November assessment, extending its recent downward movement. Meanwhile, the FBX Global Container Freight Index increased 1% to US$3,485. The Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) all declined in their 13 November readings. The NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) presented a more varied picture, with increases on Asia-US West Coast, Asia-North Europe and Transatlantic Westbound, contrasting with declines on Asia-US East Coast and Transatlantic Eastbound. Chinese freight indexes decline The SCFI decreased 1.68% to 3,572.33 points on 13 November, compared with 3,633.45 in the previous assessment. The CCFI declined approximately 0.28% to 1,919.27 points from 1,924.69 a week earlier, reversing the increase recorded in the preceding reading. The NCFI fell approximately 1.18% to 2,414.46 points, compared with 2,443.24 previously. All three Chinese composite benchmarks therefore moved lower, although the extent of the declines varied. The SCFI recorded the largest percentage decrease, followed by the NCFI, while the CCFI showed a relatively limited adjustment. NYFI shows contrasting Transpacific movements The NYFI assessment published on 13 November revealed different developments across the two major Transpacific routes. Asia-US West Coast increased 0.64% to 7,874.07, compared with 7,823.86 a week earlier, extending the route’s recent upward movement. Asia-US East Coast, however, declined 3.71% to 9,727.11 from 10,101.42 in the previous assessment. The contrast was notable because the West Coast continued to record modest gains while the East Coast experienced a more substantial weekly decrease. On Asia-North Europe, the NYFI increased 1.84% to 3,228.59 from 3,170.40, reversing the previous week’s 1.04% decline. The increase suggests a firmer latest reading for the route, although its recent weekly movements have alternated between gains and losses. Transatlantic rates move in opposite directions The NYFI also recorded diverging movements across the Transatlantic market. Westbound rates increased 1.76% to 2,890.15 from 2,840.25, recovering part of the decrease recorded in the preceding assessment. Eastbound rates continued to decline, falling 3.83% to 1,017.84 from 1,058.39. The latest Eastbound decrease followed a 5.86% decline in the previous week, extending the downward movement on the route. Overall, three of the five NYFI trade lanes recorded increases, while two declined. The movements underline the importance of examining individual routes rather than relying exclusively on composite benchmarks. Drewry WCI extends downward movement Drewry’s WCI declined 2% to US$4,305 per 40-foot container on 12 November, compared with US$4,389 in the previous assessment. The decrease reflected weaker freight rates on both the Transpacific and Asia-Europe trade lanes. Shanghai-Los Angeles fell 2% to US$7,416 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-New York declined 3% to US$9,020. On Asia-Europe, Shanghai-Rotterdam decreased 3% to US$3,504 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-Genoa remained stable at US$4,168. According to Drewry’s latest assessment , carriers are continuing to adjust available capacity through blank sailings. On the Transpacific, eight blank sailings were announced for the following week, compared with four in the current week. Drewry expects further downward pressure on freight rates amid weak demand. On Asia-Europe, eight blank sailings were announced for the following week, compared with five in the current week. Carriers have also announced higher Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates and Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) for the second half of November. Drewry expects these capacity adjustments and announced increases to provide some support to Asia-Europe rates in the coming weeks, although the actual outcome remains uncertain. FBX Global Index edges higher The FBX Global Container Freight Index increased approximately 1% to US$3,485, compared with US$3,452 in the preceding assessment. The increase followed two consecutive weekly declines, indicating a modest recovery in the global benchmark. However, the movement contrasted with the continued decline in Drewry’s WCI and the negative readings recorded by all three Chinese composite indexes. The difference reinforces the need to consider the methodologies and market coverage of each benchmark when assessing overall freight rate developments. Asia-Europe and Transpacific assessments diverge The latest figures reveal particularly interesting differences between the NYFI and Drewry assessments. On Asia-North Europe, NYFI increased 1.84%, while Drewry’s Shanghai-Rotterdam route declined 3%. Similarly, NYFI Asia-US West Coast rose 0.64%, contrasting with the 2% decrease recorded by Drewry on Shanghai-Los Angeles. On the US East Coast, however, both benchmarks indicated weaker conditions. NYFI Asia-US East Coast declined 3.71%, while Drewry Shanghai-New York fell 3%. These differences should not be interpreted as direct contradictions. NYFI is based on reported transactions involving containers that have actually shipped, while Drewry’s WCI assesses spot freight rates across selected routes. Their methodologies, route definitions and reporting periods differ, meaning the two indexes can reflect different short-term developments within related markets. Market outlook The latest assessments indicate continued weakness across several major container freight benchmarks, although individual trade lanes are not moving uniformly. The WCI recorded another weekly decline, while SCFI, CCFI and NCFI also moved lower. In contrast, the FBX recovered slightly and three NYFI routes posted increases. Drewry expects continued pressure on Transpacific freight rates amid weak demand, despite carriers’ efforts to manage capacity through blank sailings. On Asia-Europe, the impact of announced FAK increases, additional surcharges and capacity adjustments will be important to monitor in subsequent assessments. For now, the latest figures point to an uneven container freight market, with broader benchmark weakness accompanied by selective improvements on individual trade lanes.

Meanwhile, the FBX Global Container Freight Index increased 1% to US$3,485.
The Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) all declined in their 13 November readings.

articles.summary: The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity...

Photo courtesy DP World The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their fuels beginning in 2030. The Department for Transport’s proposal , published Monday, November 16, would establish a fuel standard broadly aligned with the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation while leaving room for adjustments as international negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) continue. Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, regardless of flag, covering approximately 5,000 vessels based on historical port-call data. The proposed framework would regulate all energy used on domestic voyages between UK ports, 50% of energy used on international voyages to and from the UK, and energy consumed by covered ships while at berth in British ports. Rather than mandating particular fuels, the regulation would establish progressively tightening limits on the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of energy consumed by ships. Operators could meet those requirements through alternative fuels, electrification and other lower-emission energy sources. The government is also considering compliance flexibility mechanisms, including pooling, banking and borrowing emissions credits, similar to provisions under FuelEU Maritime. However, several important details remain undecided, including how quickly emissions limits would tighten and whether the UK should follow the EU’s trajectory, align with future IMO standards or establish its own targets. The government expects the regulation to take effect from 2030. The UK Chamber of Shipping welcomed the consultation but urged policymakers to ensure that new requirements reflect the availability of alternative fuels, supporting infrastructure and commercially viable technologies. “We welcome the Government moving forward with this consultation. Greater long-term certainty can help unlock the investment needed to decarbonise shipping, but regulation needs to develop alongside the fuels, infrastructure and technology that operators will need,” a Chamber spokesperson said. “Any future UK framework must be practical, support investment and maintain the international competitiveness of UK shipping.” The Chamber has previously called for a regulatory framework that avoids duplicating existing international requirements while providing operators with sufficient flexibility to manage the transition. In an October policy paper, the organization recommended aligning fuel certification and lifecycle emissions accounting with emerging IMO standards, developing reliable monitoring and verification systems, and setting targets based on realistic assessments of fuel availability and infrastructure readiness. Those concerns are particularly relevant given the significant overlap between ships trading to the UK and those already subject to European regulations. According to the government’s consultation, approximately 97% of ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that called at UK ports in 2019 also called at EU ports. The consultation comes as the international shipping industry continues to grapple with uncertainty surrounding the IMO’s proposed global Net-Zero Framework. While the UK government acknowledges that international regulation remains the most effective way to reduce shipping emissions, it argues that uncertainty over global measures should not prevent domestic action. The proposed fuel regulation would complement the UK’s existing maritime carbon-pricing measures, including the extension of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to domestic shipping in July 2026. The government is also seeking industry feedback on whether smaller ships should eventually be included, with vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage remaining under review. Beyond the emissions requirements themselves, the consultation examines the availability of alternative maritime fuels, bunkering infrastructure, port readiness and the investment needed to support widespread adoption. The Department for Transport has emphasized that its proposals are preliminary and that no final regulatory decisions have been made. The consultation remains open until February 22, 2027 . The UK Chamber of Shipping said it will work with its members and the UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition to develop a detailed response addressing the operational, commercial and technical implications of the proposed framework. articles.title: Supertanker Rates Plunge More Than 60% From Record Highs
articles.summary: The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche LONDON, Nov 16 (Reuters) – The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October. Freight ?rates for supertankers, also known as very large crude carriers (VLCCs), carrying ?oil from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to about 308 ?on the Worldscale basis on November 13, down by 64% from their record high of 841 on October 8, Baltic Exchange data shows. The plunge in rates came as Gulf oil exporters increased crude flows towards levels seen before the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The increase in flows has been achieved using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers and so-called dark crossings, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade detection, even as attacks against ships continued. The rise in Gulf oil exports reduced demand for crude shipped from other regions, freeing up VLCCs. “Gulf oil exports recently recovered to near prewar volumes, reducing Asian buyer demand for US and North Sea crudes, which in turn weighed on demand for tankers,” said Arrow Shipbroking analyst Delia He. Vortexa analyst Ioannis Papadimitriou said the recent spike in freight rates had reduced Asian demand for longer-haul US, West African and North Sea crude, which in turn increased the region’s use of Middle East crude, and that VLCC demand for longer voyages dropped as a result. “At the same time, vessel availability is building as ships discharge in East Asia,” he said. “As more tonnage is freed up, rates come under downward pressure.” EASING GEOPOLITICAL RISK PREMIUM Rates fell even more sharply on other routes, such as from West Africa to Asia. The jump in freight costs had been partly driven by factors including the perception of a higher risk of operating in the Middle East Gulf as Iran and the US attacked tankers, which had also pushed up oil prices. Oil prices LCOc1 have dropped by 20% this month, partly on the potential for de-escalation in the Iran war. “The sharp decline in freight rates is only partly driven by market fundamentals, as such a steep move reflects an exaggerated unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium,” Arrow’s He said. articles.title: ExxonMobil brings online its fifth oil project offshore Guyana
articles.summary: The start-up of production at Uaru raises Guyana’s installed capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 16, 2026 · 6 minutes ago ExxonMobil brings online its fifth oil project offshore Guyana The start-up of production at Uaru raises Guyana’s installed capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FPSO Errea Wittu Source: MODEC ExxonMobil Guyana, a subsidiary of the U.S.-headquartered energy giant ExxonMobil, has put into production mode its fifth development in the Stabroek block off the coast of Guyana. A floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessel, which was constructed for deployment on this project, marks MODEC’s entry into Guyana's market, building on the company’s extensive experience in Brazil. ExxonMobil Guyana has confirmed the first oil from Uaru , its fifth development in the Stabroek block, lifting the country’s installed production capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day, as the FPSO Errea Wittu joins the Destiny , Unity , Prosperity , and One Guyana units. " The startup of Errea Wittu is another major milestone for Guyana and ExxonMobil. In just over a decade, Guyana has become one of the world’s fastest-growing and most important new sources of energy supply. Reaching 1.1 million barrels per day of installed capacity reflects the strength of this world-class resource, the success of our collaboration with the government and our co-venturers, and the contributions of thousands of Guyanese helping to build the country’s energy future. " — Dan Ammann ExxonMobil’s Upstream Company President Related Articles Fossil Energy MODEC’s FPSO reaches Guyana as ExxonMobil’s fifth oil project nears start-up 4 min read The Uaru field is estimated to hold more than 800 million barrels of oil. The FPSO Errea Wittu, deployed approximately 200 kilometers offshore Guyana at a water depth of 1,690 meters using a SOFEC spread mooring system, will be able to store around 2 million barrels of crude oil. This FPSO , said to mean “abundance” in the Warrau language, is expected to achieve its initial production capacity of 250,000 barrels per day in the first quarter of 2027. The operator emphasizes that Uaru marks another significant step in the development of the Stabroek block, which the company describes as one of the world’s most prolific offshore discoveries. ExxonMobil Guyana operates the Stabroek block and has a 45% interest, with Hess Guyana Exploration, part of Chevron, owning 30%, and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana holding the remaining 25%. Since 2015, the firm and its Stabroek block co-venturers have spent more than $3.9 billion with Guyanese vendors, supporting local businesses, workforce development, and economic growth. ExxonMobil recently made a final investment decision (FID) on Longtail , its eighth development on the Stabroek block. articles.summary: The Western Dredging Association (WEDA) announced the establishment of the WEDA Canada Chapter, creating a national platform dedicated to advancing collaboration, technical excellence, education, and professional engagement across Canada's dredging…
articles.body: WEDA Establishes Canadian Chapter Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 © WEDA The Western Dredging Association (WEDA) announced the establishment of the WEDA Canada Chapter, creating a national platform dedicated to advancing collaboration, technical excellence, education, and professional engagement across Canada's dredging, marine construction, navigation, sediment management, and waterways sectors. The chapter was conceived during discussions held at the Dredging Summit & Expo (DS&E) in Montréal, where industry leaders, government representatives, consultants, contractors, suppliers, port authorities, and project owners came together to explore opportunities for greater cooperation and knowledge sharing within Canada's marine infrastructure community. The WEDA Canada Chapter will serve as a forum for industry professionals from across the country to exchange expertise, address shared challenges, and promote best practices through technical programming, training initiatives, networking opportunities, and industry engagement activities. With participation expected from stakeholders representing diverse regions and disciplines, the chapter will help strengthen connections across Canada's evolving marine and dredging sectors. Canada's marine infrastructure industry plays a vital role in supporting trade, navigation, environmental stewardship, resource development, and coastal resilience. The new chapter will provide an important mechanism for bringing together professionals and organizations working across these sectors while fostering dialogue on the opportunities and challenges unique to the Canadian market. As the chapter develops, it will explore opportunities to host educational programs, technical workshops, conferences, and networking events designed to deliver value to members and support the continued advancement of Canada's marine infrastructure industry.

November 16, 2026 © Star International Star International and LALIZAS UK have been awarded a contract to supply lifejackets to the Royal Navy, following a procurement, evaluation and testing process. The award follows a two-and-a-half-year program, during which BAE Systems, as the prime supplier, selected Star International in partnership with LALIZAS UK as the contract partners for the provision of lifesaving equipment. The program involved the assessment and selection of LALIZAS lifejackets for a wide range of Royal Navy applications. This includes commercially available models for use in training and water-activity centres, as well as bespoke lifejacket solutions designed to meet the requirements of personnel serving aboard Royal Navy vessels. Star International and LALIZAS UK specialists also worked closely with Royal Navy personnel, providing product familiarization and training to support the use of the selected equipment.

articles.title: Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd Expand Suez Canal Return With Three More Gemini Services
articles.summary: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are bringing three more Gemini Cooperation services back through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, marking another major step in the container shipping industry’s gradual return to...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Suez Canal Authority/Handout via REUTERS Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are bringing three more Gemini Cooperation services back through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, marking another major step in the container shipping industry’s gradual return to the shorter route between Asia and Europe. The carriers announced Monday that their AE1, AE2 and AE3 services will shift from sailing around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to transiting the Suez Canal, with the changes taking effect between December 2026 and January 2027. The announcement builds on a series of earlier routing changes as the partners progressively restore Suez transits across their shared network. According to Maersk’s November 16 advisory, the transitions will begin with the AE2 service on December 4, followed by AE3 on December 20 and AE1 on January 14, 2027. The AE2 service, connecting Asia, Europe and the Middle East, will begin its revised rotation with the Mary Maersk departing from Ningbo. The AE3 service will follow with the Alette Maersk from Shanghai, while the AE1 transition will begin with the Damietta Express, also from Shanghai. The decision follows a broader return to the Suez corridor that has gathered momentum in recent months. In September, the two carriers announced the rerouting of four additional Gemini services — AE5, AE11, AE12 and ME2 — joining two services already using the canal. Earlier this month, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd also announced the return of their ME1 service connecting India and Europe, with the first revised sailings scheduled for November 4 and 13. The latest changes extend that shift to more of the carriers’ main Asia-Europe services, reducing reliance on the significantly longer route around southern Africa. For container lines and shippers, the Suez route offers shorter voyages, lower fuel consumption and faster transit times compared with Cape of Good Hope diversions. Returning services to the canal can also free up vessel capacity that has been tied up by longer voyages. Still, the carriers stressed that the return remains dependent on regional security conditions. articles.summary: Saronic Technologies has selected Norway-based Syncrolift to design and supply what is expected to be the world's largest shiplift and vessel transfer system for Port Alpha, its planned $3 billion shipyard development in Brownsville, Texas.The contract…
articles.body: Saronic taps Syncrolift for Port Alpha Shiplift Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 Rolf-Atle Tomassen, Managing Director of Syncrolift AS; Chris Brinkley, VP of International at Saronic; and Ole Falk Hansen, CEO of Nekkar ASA, commemorated the signing of the shiplift contract in Oslo on November 11, 2026, on the sidelines of the Atlantic Future Forum. Image courtesy Saronic Saronic Technologies has selected Norway-based Syncrolift to design and supply what is expected to be the world's largest shiplift and vessel transfer system for Port Alpha, its planned $3 billion shipyard development in Brownsville, Texas. The contract, valued at more than $100 million, calls for a shiplift featuring a 300-meter platform and lifting capacity of 67,000 tonnes, more than twice the capacity of the next-largest installation, according to Saronic. The system will serve as a centerpiece of Port Alpha's production strategy, which emphasizes high-throughput construction of autonomous and conventionally crewed vessels for commercial and defense customers. Rather than relying on traditional graving docks, Port Alpha will employ a production model allowing multiple ships to be assembled and outfitted simultaneously on land before being transferred to the shiplift for launching. Syncrolift's tandem lifting system will incorporate a rigid platform, condition-monitoring technology and digital-twin controls to support safe vessel movements and lifting operations. "Syncrolift's technology and track record made them the right supplier to deliver a system that is strategically important to how we're approaching Port Alpha and the reindustrialization of U.S. shipbuilding," said Doug Lambert, Saronic Co-Founder and COO. The Port Alpha development initially encompasses 835 acres, with potential expansion to nearly 4,400 acres. Saronic projects the shipyard could create up to 10,000 direct jobs. Syncrolift will manage the project from its headquarters in Vestby, Norway. The award was announced in conjunction with the Atlantic Future Forum, highlighting Saronic's strategy of incorporating technologies and equipment from allied nations into its U.S. shipbuilding operations. The investment reflects Saronic's ambition to increase domestic shipbuilding capacity through automated production processes, advanced vessel-handling infrastructure and parallel construction methods intended to accelerate deliveries.

articles.body: ICS: Geopolitical Tensions Threaten Global Shipping, Freedom of Navigation Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 ICS Chairman John Denholm. Image courtesy ICS The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) has warned that escalating geopolitical tensions, regional conflicts and increasing regulatory fragmentation threaten freedom of navigation and the stability of global maritime trade. Speaking at the third Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit on November 16, ICS Chairman John Denholm called for renewed international commitment to maritime law and a rules-based trading system, warning that disruptions to established shipping routes and growing protectionism could undermine global supply chains. "We are seeing geopolitical tensions reshape trade flows, conflicts disrupting established shipping routes, greater competition between major economies, and a growing tendency towards unilateral measures and regional regulation," Denholm told more than 250 delegates. He emphasized that shipping, responsible for transporting approximately 90% of global trade by volume, remains fundamental to international economic stability, food security and energy supplies. The summit, organized by ICS in cooperation with Hong Kong's Transport and Logistics Bureau and Hong Kong Shipowners Association, brought together government officials, shipowners and maritime industry executives under the theme "Navigating Risk – Partnering for Resilience." Discussions focused on the economic consequences of maritime disruptions, including rising transportation costs, delayed cargo deliveries and supply chain vulnerabilities. Hong Kong Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan emphasized that strengthening maritime resilience requires cooperation across governments and industries. "In an era of redrawn trade lanes, geopolitical friction and climate urgency, no single jurisdiction or sector can build supply chain resilience alone," Chan said. The summit concluded with calls for stronger international cooperation to protect seafarers, preserve freedom of navigation and maintain reliable global shipping networks. articles.title: Jones Act Waiver Extended Another 90 Days as U.S. Maritime Groups Sound Alarm
articles.summary: The Trump administration has extended its emergency Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue transporting oil and other commodities between U.S. ports under a case-by-case...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network By Igor Karasi / Shutterstock The Trump administration has extended its emergency Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue transporting oil and other commodities between U.S. ports under a case-by-case approval process, despite growing opposition from the domestic maritime industry. The extension, confirmed Friday by U.S. Customs and Border Protection , takes effect November 16 and runs through February 14, 2027, prolonging what has become the longest-running waiver in the history of the century-old shipping law. CBP said the Department of Homeland Security approved the third extension of the waiver originally issued March 17 at the request of the Department of War. Covered cargo must be loaded aboard an authorized vessel before 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on February 14. The Jones Act generally requires cargo transported between U.S. ports to move aboard American-built, American-owned and American-crewed vessels. The administration first suspended those requirements for certain commodities in March as the war with Iran disrupted global energy markets and pushed fuel prices higher. The White House has defended the waiver as a way to ease transportation bottlenecks and increase shipping flexibility. The administration initially issued a blanket waiver before moving in August to a more restrictive, voyage-by-voyage approval process following criticism from U.S. maritime operators, shipbuilders and lawmakers. That process remains in place under the latest extension. Companies seeking to use foreign-flagged vessels must first submit a request identifying the vessel, cargo, proposed voyage and national defense justification. The Maritime Administration (MARAD) then conducts a market survey to determine whether a Jones Act-qualified vessel is available to perform the transportation. The Department of War makes the final determination on whether the waiver applies to the proposed voyage. The extension drew immediate criticism from U.S. maritime industry groups, which argue that continued exemptions undermine the administration’s stated goal of rebuilding American shipbuilding and strengthening the domestic fleet. The American Maritime Partnership (AMP) called for the waiver to end while urging strict enforcement of the existing approval process. “AMP calls for a prompt end to the waiver and looks forward to working with the Administration to advance our shared goal of restoring American maritime dominance by unleashing investment in rebuilding and growing the U.S. domestic fleet,” the organization said. AMP urged officials to ensure that individual exemptions meet the statutory standard of military necessity and are not used to displace American vessels and mariners on routine commercial voyages. The group also stressed that foreign operators receiving waivers remain subject to applicable U.S. tax, immigration and employment laws. The Offshore Marine Service Association (OMSA), which represents 170 companies and approximately 12,000 American workers, issued a sharper warning, arguing that repeated exemptions are eroding confidence in the domestic maritime industry. “The offshore industry has seen this happen before. Every exception gets sold as temporary, and every one leaves fewer opportunities for American vessels and mariners,” said OMSA President and CEO Aaron Smith. “What started as a 60-day measure is now heading into its ninth month, and it still hasn’t delivered. Every extension tells investors the market for American vessels can disappear on the whim of a bureaucrat, and that investment goes overseas.” OMSA also raised concerns about transparency in the case-by-case approval process, arguing that information about approved movements is frequently published weeks or months after the cargo has moved. Although MARAD publishes reports covering waiver voyages , OMSA says the delayed disclosure makes meaningful oversight difficult. “The public still can’t see who is asking, what’s being approved, or why,” Smith said. “When the data does come out, it comes out in clumps, long after the cargo has moved. That isn’t an oversight. That’s a paper trail written after the fact.” The association compared the current waiver to decades of regulatory exceptions affecting the U.S. offshore energy industry, which it argues have allowed foreign vessels to capture work that would otherwise support American operators and mariners. The latest extension sets up another three months of tension between the administration’s efforts to ease domestic fuel transportation costs and its broader push to restore American maritime capabilities. For now, foreign-flagged vessels will remain eligible for approved domestic shipments through mid-February, while U.S. maritime groups continue pressing Washington to bring the emergency exemption to an end. articles.title: CIMAC Calls for Global IMO Net-Zero Framework
articles.summary: CIMAC is calling for the development and adoption of a global International Maritime Organization (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, warning that growing regulatory uncertainty threatens to slow investment in alternative fuels, propulsion technologies…
articles.body: CIMAC Calls for Global IMO Net-Zero Framework Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 CIMAC is calling for the development and adoption of a global International Maritime Organization (IMO) Net-Zero Framework , warning that growing regulatory uncertainty threatens to slow investment in alternative fuels, propulsion technologies and supporting maritime infrastructure. CIMAC's Greenhouse Gas Strategy Group said the shipping industry's transition toward lower emissions requires a predictable, globally aligned regulatory environment that provides clear guidance for shipowners, engine manufacturers, fuel suppliers, ports and technology developers. Central to CIMAC's position is the need for clarity on future emissions compliance mechanisms, fuel accounting, incentives and carbon costs. Without these, the industry faces considerable uncertainty when evaluating investments in new vessels, alternative fuels and related infrastructure. CIMAC also cautioned against fragmented regional regulations, which could create conflicting compliance requirements and certification standards for an inherently international industry. The organization advocates a technology-neutral approach, allowing different fuels and propulsion systems to contribute to emissions reductions based on their verified greenhouse-gas performance. While the development and availability of sustainable marine fuels remain significant challenges, CIMAC emphasized that improvements in vessel and propulsion efficiency can deliver immediate emissions reductions. Technical and operational efficiency measures can also reduce future demand for alternative fuels, helping ease pressure on supply as production capacity expands. CIMAC maintains that an effective IMO framework, combined with continued improvements in energy efficiency, is essential to establish viable business cases for decarbonization investments and provide the maritime industry with a consistent, long-term pathway toward net-zero emissions.

articles.title: Molslinjen Electric Ferries taps AYK Energy for Battery Power
articles.summary: AYK Energy has secured what it describes as the largest marine battery contract in ferry industry history, supplying 165 MWh of battery capacity for three fully electric high-speed catamarans being built by Incat Tasmania for Danish ferry operator…
articles.body: Molslinjen Electric Ferries taps AYK Energy for Battery Power Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 Image courtesy Incat Tasmania AYK Energy has secured what it describes as the largest marine battery contract in ferry industry history, supplying 165 MWh of battery capacity for three fully electric high-speed catamarans being built by Incat Tasmania for Danish ferry operator Molslinjen. Each vessel will be equipped with a 55 MWh installation of AYK Energy's DNV type-approved Polaris lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery system, supporting operating speeds of up to 40 knots and high-capacity charging in approximately 30 minutes. The contract was signed with Wärtsilä , which is serving as systems integrator and will supply the vessels' integrated electric propulsion systems and waterjets. The three catamarans, designed to carry up to 1,500 passengers and 500 cars each, will operate across Denmark's Kattegat between Jutland and Zealand. Upon entering service, they are expected to become Europe's largest electric ferries. The first vessel is scheduled to arrive in Denmark in late 2027 and begin operations in the first quarter of 2028, with the remaining two vessels expected to arrive in 2028 and 2029. A central technical challenge was reducing battery weight while maintaining the energy capacity and power output required for high-speed ferry operations. According to AYK founder Chris Kruger, when Molslinjen began evaluating battery suppliers nearly two years ago, the company's proposed battery installation weighed more than 700 tonnes. Through redesign and advances in battery technology, AYK reduced that figure to less than 400 tonnes for the first vessel, a reduction exceeding 40%. AYK founder Chris Kruger. Image courtesy AYK The redesign incorporates new battery cells, manufacturing techniques adapted from the automotive industry and a lighter aluminum structure intended to improve energy density without compromising performance. "We decided to rethink the battery's design from the ground up to reduce weight and improve performance," Kruger said. "With new battery cells, inspiration from manufacturing techniques in the automotive industry and a lighter, stronger aluminium structure, we can store more energy per kilogram and deliver more power." The Polaris system also incorporates AYK's proprietary fire suppression and thermal management technologies. Kruger emphasized that safety remains a primary consideration in developing higher-capacity marine battery systems, particularly given the operating conditions and evacuation challenges associated with passenger vessels. Molslinjen CEO Carsten Jensen said the reduction in battery weight was instrumental in selecting AYK. "We are pushing the boundaries of technology here, and the combined weight of the vessel and its batteries will be crucial to operating such large vessels at high speed across the Kattegat," Jensen said. Wärtsilä's Dr. Torsten Büssow noted that large electric ferries require a careful balance between rapid, high-power charging, sufficient stored energy for longer crossings and the weight limitations of aluminum catamaran construction. The Molslinjen order adds to AYK's expanding marine battery portfolio, which includes a contract for Germany's new polar research vessel Polarstern, two 12 MWh Orion+ installations aboard Brittany Ferries' hybrid-electric vessels Guillaume de Normandie and Saint-Malo, and a 6 MWh battery system for Svitzer's battery-methanol tug. The contract highlights the growing scale of marine electrification, with battery capacity, charging infrastructure and system weight increasingly determining the feasibility of fully electric operations on demanding commercial ferry routes. Image courtesy Incat Tasmania

articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) will revise its Emergency Fuel Surcharge (EFS) across long-haul and short-sea trades from 15 December 2026. The updated surcharge will apply to dry and refrigerated cargo, with different levels for long-haul headhaul and backhaul shipments. Under the revised structure, dry containers moving on long-haul headhaul trades will be subject to an EFS of US$180 per TEU. The corresponding charge for reefer cargo will be US$230 per TEU. For long-haul backhaul movements, ONE will apply a surcharge of US$90 per TEU for dry containers and US$115 per TEU for reefers. The same US$90 and US$115 rates will apply to dry and reefer cargo, respectively, across all short-sea trades. The FMC scope includes the United States, American Samoa, Puerto Rico, Guam, Saipan and Hawaii. The same implementation date will also apply to Canada. November 16, 2026 Image courtesy Cool Carriers Cool Carriers held a naming and launch ceremony for its newest vessel, Cool Eternity, recently at Shikoku Shipyard in Japan. Cool Eternity is the latest addition to the Cool Carriers fleet. Designed to transport fresh fruit and other perishable cargo, the vessel measures 189.9 metres in length and 30.7 metres in breadth. Her five refrigerated holds provide approximately 905,000 cubic feet of cargo capacity across nine cooling zones. In addition to carrying a full cargo of palletised bananas below deck, Cool Eternity can accommodate approximately 300 loaded 40-foot refrigerated containers on deck and hatch covers. Cool Eternity is fitted with an exhaust gas cleaning system, commonly known as a scrubber. It removes sulphur oxides from the ship’s exhaust before they reach the atmosphere. Reducing these emissions helps protect air quality in ports and coastal communities and limits the ship’s contribution to acid rain. Chris Plocienniczak, USA General Manager at Cool Carriers, performed the naming ceremony. Reflecting on the occasion, he said: “I am immensely proud to have had the honour of naming this vessel today. What a remarkable achievement for Cool Carriers!” “We congratulate the team at Shikoku Shipyard and everyone involved in bringing Cool Eternity to launch day. We wish her and her future crews fair winds and safe seas”. The ceremony follows the launch of Cool Emerald at the same shipyard as part of Cool Carriers' ongoing newbuilding program. These new vessels form part of Cool Carriers' long-term fleet renewal strategy, strengthening its competitiveness in the specialised reefer market while supporting improved operational efficiency and environmental performance. “We will continue to support our customers and partners by building ships with exceptional fuel efficiency and environmental performance,” said Chris Plocienniczak.

articles.title: Höegh Autoliners partners with BYD for battery-powered Aurora vessel
articles.summary: Höegh Autoliners has signed an agreement with BYD Energy Storage to install marine battery systems on its upcoming Aurora No. 12 car carrier. The project will combine battery storage, solar panels and a shaft generator with propulsion capable of using ammonia. The companies signed the strategic and technical...
articles.body: Höegh Autoliners has signed an agreement with BYD Energy Storage to install marine battery systems on its upcoming Aurora No. 12 car carrier. The project will combine battery storage, solar panels and a shaft generator with propulsion capable of using ammonia. The companies signed the strategic and technical cooperation agreement on 9 November 2026 during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Aurora No. 12 is scheduled for delivery and the start of commercial operations in May 2028. According to Höegh Autoliners, the vessel will be the first deep-sea car carrier to combine these energy technologies in a single integrated system. The installation is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 1,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent annually. However, this remains a projected reduction rather than an achieved operational result. Battery integration to improve onboard energy efficiency The new system will combine BYD Energy Storage batteries with a shaft generator and solar panels. Together, these technologies are intended to improve energy management and reduce fuel consumption. The vessel will also be equipped with propulsion technology capable of operating on ammonia from delivery. Ammonia does not produce CO₂ during combustion. However, its overall environmental performance depends on how the fuel is produced and on the management of other emissions associated with its use. Green ammonia also remains more expensive than conventional marine fuels, creating an additional challenge for its wider adoption. “This shows that shipping can take the lead in the green transition. We are combining every green technology available on one vessel capable of running on ammonia from day one. Nobody has done that on a deep-sea car carrier before,” said Andreas Enger, CEO, Höegh Autoliners. The cooperation will also allow both companies to gain operational experience with integrated energy systems for large ocean-going vessels. According to Höegh Autoliners, the project forms part of its wider efforts to develop lower-emission deep-sea transportation. Aurora Class programme expands to 18 vessels Aurora No. 12 belongs to Höegh Autoliners’ Aurora Class, a new generation of pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs). Each vessel can transport up to 9,100 cars. The company states that the class can reduce carbon emissions by up to 58% compared with conventional PCTCs. The vessels carry DNV ammonia-ready and methanol-ready notations, supporting the company’s transition towards alternative marine fuels. China Merchants Heavy Industry (Jiangsu) is building the Aurora fleet, while Everllence supplies the main engines. Other project partners include Kongsberg Maritime, DNV and vessel designer Deltamarin. Following an order for six additional ships in August 2026, the Aurora programme now comprises 18 vessels. Further options and reserved construction slots could increase the programme to 26 vessels. The latest battery agreement adds another technology to the fleet renewal programme. Höegh Autoliners aims to use the combination of alternative fuels and energy-efficient systems to reduce emissions from long-distance vehicle transportation.

(Courtesy of Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries) South Korea’s first container ship trial along the Northern Sea Route exposed the challenges of Arctic navigation, with crew members describing a near-abandonment decision after drifting ice blocked their path. The operator is now considering selling the vessel after a single round trip, reportedly negotiating a potential sale back to its former owner, HMM. The South Korean vessel’s struggles also exposes the experience gap with China. Chinese operators have spent several years building experience running container ships through the Arctic , while PanStar was making its first attempt. The voyage underscored how operational experience can be just as important as a vessel’s ice-class capabilities. “When we were trapped by countless ice floes, I thought we might not be able to continue the voyage. There were many unexpected situations every day,” first officer Park Ji-jeong said at an October 22 press briefing hosted by South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries. “I am relieved that we ultimately returned safely.” The PanStar Acro , a 2,758-TEU container ship, encountered drifting ice south of Wrangel Island in the Chukchi Sea during the night of August 31 into September 1. “The ice was drifting in large quantities. We could not see ahead and had to rely solely on radar,” Park said. “The situation was difficult enough that it was hard to continue sailing, but fortunately visibility improved after some time and we were able to move again.” Captain Seo Myeong-won said the crew considered turning back. Rather than attempting to navigate blindly, he consulted with an ice pilot and decided to wait for daylight. “If we could not find a route because it was dark, I judged it would be better to check again when daylight came,” Seo said in an interview published by the South Korean government. “We waited without moving recklessly, and about three hours later the route became visible.” The episode is reflected in the vessel’s AIS track. On August 31, the Acro slowed and maneuvered back and forth for several hours southeast of Wrangel Island. The Centre for High North Logistics, analyzing Kpler/MarineTraffic data, estimated that the vessel made only about 16 nautical miles of westward progress during the episode, adding approximately eight hours to its transit. The ship also encountered large ice floes near Vilkitsky Strait and experienced cold-weather equipment problems affecting fuel and lubricating-oil circulation. It completed both Arctic passages without icebreaker assistance, but the voyage exposed limitations in its suitability for sustained polar operations. PanStar is considering selling or chartering out the Acro and acquiring a more ice-capable, fuel-efficient vessel for further Arctic trials in 2027. Korean media reported that HMM, which sold the vessel to PanStar in August, is the prospective buyer and that price negotiations are underway. No agreement has been announced. The proposed sale comes as PanStar Line faces mounting financial pressure. Its debt-to-equity ratio rose to 336.5% in 2025, with borrowings reaching KRW 140.2 billion ($100 million), according to financial publication The Bell. The company has not disclosed the Acro ‘s purchase price or expected resale value. The voyage also fell short of its commercial ambitions. The ship carried just 737 TEU of loaded exports and returned with 1,743 TEU of empty containers , without securing import cargo. The Korea Shipowners’ Association provided KRW 3 billion in basic voyage support and offered up to another KRW 1 billion tied to round-trip cargo volumes exceeding 2,000 TEU. Whether empty containers count toward the threshold remains unknown. South Korea’s government, meanwhile, has reaffirmed its commitment to Arctic shipping . In a statement, Oceans Minister Hwang Jong-woo called the trial a “meaningful achievement” in demonstrating the potential of a new maritime route using a container ship carrying Korean exports. “We will continue preparing so that this achievement leads to the next voyage and the Northern Sea Route can become a new opportunity for our economy,” he said. For PanStar, replacing the Acro may be necessary to continue the project. But the first voyage also demonstrated that an ice-class vessel alone will not guarantee reliable operations. China’s accumulated experience suggests that developing the expertise to interpret ice conditions, manage unexpected situations, and maintain schedules will be just as important. articles.summary: Guinea is seeking backing from US, Chinese and multilateral financiers for a planned $1.9 billion deep-water port, its mines minister told Reuters, aiming to build on the giant Simandou iron ore project and turn the country into a regional trade hub.

REUTERS/Souleymane Camara By Maxwell Akalaare Adombila CONAKRY, Nov 16 (Reuters) – Guinea is seeking backing from US, Chinese and multilateral financiers for a planned $1.9 billion deep-water port, its mines minister told Reuters, aiming to build on the giant Simandou iron ore project and turn the country into a regional trade hub. The project would be among Africa’s largest, and marks Guinea’s latest effort to leverage its vast mineral wealth following the launch of the Simandou project and comes as governments and investors compete for influence over infrastructure supporting global mineral supply chains. Mines Minister Bouna Sylla said the government had completed feasibility studies and was engaging a broad group of potential financiers, including the US International Development Finance Corporation, Chinese investors, the World Bank, the African Development Bank, Africa Finance Corporation and the International Finance Corporation. He did not provide a timeline for selecting investors or starting construction of the project, which has a planned 20-metre draft capable of handling 200,000-metric-ton Capesize vessels. BIGGEST PROJECT SINCE SIMANDOU The port would be Guinea’s biggest infrastructure project since Simandou, the roughly $20 billion iron ore development that shipped its first output last year after decades of delays. The project, jointly developed by Rio Tinto RIO.L, RIO.AX, China’s Baowu Steel and other partners, includes a 600-kilometre (373-mile) railway and deep-water export terminal. While Simandou’s infrastructure was designed primarily to transport iron ore from one of the world’s largest untapped deposits, the proposed port is intended as a multi-user facility serving miners, container traffic and industrial operators, Sylla said, reflecting Guinea’s broader goal of converting its mineral wealth into a platform for trade. “Simandou has shown the importance of large-scale infrastructure,” he said. “Our objective now is to develop infrastructure that can support mining, trade and industrial development on a much broader scale.” Guinea, the world’s largest bauxite producer, has largely seen mining companies build dedicated railways and export terminals tailored to individual projects. The new port would mark a shift towards shared infrastructure that could also serve other industries and regional users. Sylla said the project’s economics should make it a compelling alternative to bauxite miners’ dedicated rail and port facilities. “It is a port for everyone,” he said. “We want to diversify the sources of funding rather than rely on a single source.” (Reporting by Maxwell Akalaare Adombila; Editing by Clara Denina and Louise Heavens) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.body: Dry Cargo Xylas wins second term at Intercargo Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 218 1 minute read Intercargo Intercargo Greek shipowner John Xylas has secured another two years at the helm of dry bulk shipping association Intercargo, with executives from Berge Bulk and Fleet Management joining its leadership team. Members meeting in Rome re-elected the Ariston Navigation president and chief executive as chairman for 2027 and 2028, extending a tenure that began in January 2025. Metaxia Psalti, chief operating officer of Greece’s Neda Maritime Agency, has also been re-elected as vice-chair, while Paolo Tonon, technical director at Berge Bulk, and Ranvijay S. Rana, product director of dry cargo operations at Fleet Management, have been elected as two new vice-chairs. The appointments take effect on January 1, 2027. The reshuffle will see Captain Uttam Kumar Jaiswal of Pacific Basin Shipping step down at the end of December after completing the maximum six consecutive years as vice-chair. Xylas, who succeeded Dimitrios Fafalios in 2025, will lead an association that has continued expanding its international reach, with membership now exceeding 500 companies and organisations for the first time. Intercargo said its members now operate more than 5,100 dry cargo vessels, up from over 4,500 ships represented at the start of 2026. “We passed 500 members for the first time,” Xylas said, pointing to the association’s growing reach across the world’s major shipping centres. The Rome meeting also approved changes to Intercargo’s structure, including the establishment of a Technical and Operations Committee from January 2027. The new body will bring together technical, operational and vetting activities under the chairmanship of Dimitris Monioudis of Rethymnis & Kulukundis, supported by Cesare d’Api of d’Amico and Psalti. Intercargo has also approved two new working groups focusing on artificial intelligence, digitalisation and crew welfare, which are expected to start work in early 2027. articles.title: Freightos receives Nasdaq warning over minimum share price requirement
articles.summary: Freightos has received a formal notification from Nasdaq after its share price remained below the exchange’s minimum requirement for continued listing. The digital freight booking and pricing company received the notice on 10 November 2026. According to Freightos, its ordinary shares had closed below US$1 for 30...
articles.body: Freightos has received a formal notification from Nasdaq after its share price remained below the exchange’s minimum requirement for continued listing. The digital freight booking and pricing company received the notice on 10 November 2026. According to Freightos, its ordinary shares had closed below US$1 for 30 consecutive business days, from 29 September to 9 November. Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2), listed companies must maintain a minimum closing bid price of US$1 per share. Freightos no longer meets this requirement and must take steps to restore compliance. However, the notification does not immediately affect the company’s Nasdaq listing or trading activities. Its shares will continue to trade on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the ticker CRGO. Freightos also confirmed that the notice does not affect its business operations. Freightos given until May 2027 to regain compliance Nasdaq has granted Freightos an initial 180-calendar-day compliance period, ending on 10 May 2027. To regain compliance, the company’s closing share price must reach at least US$1 for a minimum of ten consecutive business days. Nasdaq may extend this period under its applicable listing rules. If Freightos meets the requirement, Nasdaq will issue written confirmation and close the matter. However, if the company fails to regain compliance before the deadline, it may qualify for an additional 180-day period, subject to Nasdaq’s requirements. Freightos said it will continue monitoring its share price while evaluating available options to address the situation. These options could include a reverse share split, which would require any necessary shareholder approval. However, the company has not announced a decision to implement such a measure. The company also acknowledged that there is no guarantee it will regain compliance within the applicable period. Freightos continues digital freight operations Freightos operates a digital platform connecting freight forwarders, shipping lines, airlines and other logistics providers. Its services include freight pricing, booking, procurement, payments and market intelligence across air, ocean and road transportation. The Nasdaq notification comes as the company continues developing its digital freight technology. On 10 November, Freightos announced an upgraded platform for freight forwarders, introducing artificial intelligence tools into pricing and booking workflows. The company also recently reported higher transaction volumes and record gross booking value for the third quarter of 2026. Nevertheless, the latest Nasdaq notice introduces a separate regulatory challenge concerning its stock market listing. Freightos will need to meet the minimum share price requirement within the permitted compliance period to avoid potential further listing proceedings.

The Design & Build agreement covers the existing 610-metre quay wall. The project will prepare the terminal for the introduction of rail-mounted ship-to-shore (STS) gantry cranes, replacing the current reliance on mobile harbour cranes. The upgrade forms part of DP World’s wider efforts to modernise its operations in Angola. It will support faster container handling and improve the terminal’s ability to accommodate larger vessels. According to EDECS, the works will include structural reinforcement, piling, crane infrastructure and utility installations. Quay upgrade to support new STS cranes Under the contract, EDECS will install 120 piles, each measuring one metre in diameter and extending up to 45 metres in length. The company will also construct a reinforced concrete back beam and extend the existing capping beam. In addition, the project includes crane rails, securing systems and related quay equipment. The works will also cover electrical infrastructure, substations, fire-fighting networks and other utilities required for the operation of the new STS cranes. EDECS will carry out several structural tests to assess the strength and reliability of the new foundations. The upgraded infrastructure is expected to improve vessel loading and unloading operations. It will also support shorter turnaround times and more efficient cargo handling. “The modernization of our quay infrastructure represents a milestone in the ongoing transformation of DP World Luanda and reinforces our commitment to improving the efficiency and competitiveness of trade through Angola,” said Francisco Pinzón, CEO, DP World Luanda. DP World continues investment in Angola The latest contract follows DP World’s announcement in October 2026 of a US$90 million expansion programme at the Port of Luanda. The wider development includes plans to extend the terminal’s quay to approximately 830 metres and increase its annual container-handling capacity from 500,000 to 1.2 million TEUs. DP World also plans to introduce three STS cranes and 12 semi-automated rubber-tyred gantry cranes as part of the expansion. The improvements are intended to allow the terminal to handle two Post-Panamax vessels simultaneously. The new contract also extends the relationship between EDECS and DP World in Africa. The companies are already working together on a port modernisation project in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. EDECS is involved in the redevelopment of cargo-handling yards and supporting infrastructure at the Tanzanian port. The Luanda agreement adds another container terminal infrastructure project to the company’s regional portfolio. The value of the latest contract and its expected completion date have not been disclosed.

The Design & Build agreement covers the existing 610-metre quay wall.
The project will prepare the terminal for the introduction of rail-mounted ship-to-shore (STS) gantry cranes, replacing the current reliance on mobile harbour cranes.

articles.title: Shell concerned over IMO delays on green bunker rules, backs mass-balanced bio-LNG
articles.summary: Prolonged discussions over new global green bunker rules will risk delaying industry investments and result in a fragmented regulatory landscape, Shell said less than two weeks ahead of the International Maritime Organization’s next round of decarbonization talks. The UN agency’s member states are due to hold talks...
articles.body: Shell concerned over IMO delays on green bunker rules, backs mass-balanced bio-LNG in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Prolonged discussions over new global green bunker rules will risk delaying industry investments and result in a fragmented regulatory landscape, Shell said less than two weeks ahead of the International Maritime Organization’s next round of decarbonization talks. The UN agency’s member states are due to hold talks over the Net-Zero Framework between Nov. 23-Dec. 4, having failed to adopt the regulation as scheduled in October 2025 due to a lack of consensus. In a Nov. 12 emailed statement to Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, the energy company said the industry needs regulatory “clarity, not perfection” before making investment decisions on low-carbon fuel plants that could operate for decades. “Further delay could mean a variety of things including regulatory fragmentation, delayed industry investment, and ultimately higher costs for industry and consumers,” Shell said. “Fragmentation is not to anyone’s benefit. We are a global industry.” The comment echoed the views of shipping industry associations, such as the International Chamber of Shipping, as the EU has ushered in several regulations to limit greenhouse gas emissions from ship operations. Moreover, the NZF should have “a durable trajectory should reflect how quickly fuels, infrastructure and technology can scale,” and be a consistent framework under which fuels and technologies compete according to verified well-to-wake GHG, according to Shell. The company also called for recognition of avoided emissions and provisions allowing companies to bank or trade compliance surpluses. Bio-LNG Credible certification and chain-of-custody rules, including mass balancing, could enable renewable fuels like biomethane injected into gas grids to be attributed to an equivalent quantity of bio-LNG without requiring physical segregation throughout the supply chain. “The objective should be to recognize verified real-world GHG performance while giving renewable fuels a practical route to scale through existing infrastructure,” Shell said. Supplying enough segregated bio-LNG to fill a ship could theoretically require around 250 truckloads, Shell said, illustrating the logistical constraints of physical delivery. “Physical segregation becomes challenging at scale, which is why mass balancing is so important,” the company said. While one of the largest producers and suppliers of conventional, oil-based marine fuels, Shell operates the world’s largest physical LNG bunker network with 16 barges delivering the fuel at 29 ports in 13 countries. The company is also able to provide bio-LNG at many of the ports, including Rotterdam, Algeciras and Miami. Shell has long argued that shipping companies with LNG-fueled ships have a pathway to achieve the IMO’s net-zero target by 2050, with the opportunities to shift to methane generated from low-carbon means. “As the fuel evolves, we don’t have to start again,” Shell said. “Bio-LNG and, in time, synthetic LNG, can use established LNG value chains and infrastructure without requiring major system changes.” Delivered bunker costs for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil averaged $17.90/gigajoule in Rotterdam in October, compared with $27.41/GJ for bioblend B30 with 30% used cooking oil methyl ester, $28.78/GJ for LNG and $51.71/GJ for bio-LNG, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator from S&P Global Energy. articles.title: MEPC85: Researcher on how first global climate deal could pave the way for fossil-free shipping
articles.summary: From November 30 to December 4, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Marine environment protection committee will resume its second extraordinary session*. The goal is to reach a consensus on the first global regulatory framework to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from shipping. A framework like this would...
articles.body: MEPC85: Researcher on how first global climate deal could pave the way for fossil-free shipping in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 From November 30 to December 4, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Marine environment protection committee will resume its second extraordinary session*. The goal is to reach a consensus on the first global regulatory framework to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from shipping. A framework like this would encourage the shipping sector to switch from fossil fuel-based marine fuels, giving lower-emission alternatives a competitive edge. The proposed framework was supposed to have been adopted in 2025, but due to strong opposition and unresolved disputes among some member states, the meeting was postponed for a year. Fayas Malik Kanchiralla, a researcher at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden says: “It is absolutely essential that all member states reach an agreement on effective global measures this time if we are to tackle carbon emissions from shipping. Without a decision, the sector risks falling short of its climate targets, and as such, emissions from the sector may continue to rise,” says Fayas Malik Kanchiralla, who is the lead author of a recent scientific study in Nature Energy, which analyses the different proposed climate regulations: Marine Fuel Choices and related life-cycle environmental impacts under global shipping policies. The research shows that the design of the regulatory framework is crucial for reaching the climate neutrality of shipping. It also highlights the benefits of combining economic incentives with fuel greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity standards, rather than focusing on greenhouse gas emissions from ships alone. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has 176 member states. In 2023, the organization adopted a revised greenhouse gas strategy setting the ambition of reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. In April 2025, IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) approved the draft Net-Zero Framework, which combines a global marine fuel greenhouse gas intensity standard with a pricing mechanism for greenhouse gas emissions – but efforts to formally adopt the framework encountered a major obstacle in October 2025. The IMO had developed a proposal for a common global regulatory framework to phase out fossil-based marine fuels, and member states were expected to adopt it. Instead, the meeting was adjourned for a year following disagreements among member states, including opposition from the United States and Saudi Arabia. As a result, there is currently no global regulatory framework governing the use of fossil fuels in shipping. Although the European Union has introduced measures to reduce emissions from shipping, international shipping operates in a global market. A common international framework could help align incentives across countries and reduce the risk that companies investing in climate-neutral fuels face a competitive disadvantage. “As things stand today, companies investing in low-emission fuels can face higher costs than competitors continuing to use fossil-based fuels. A well-designed global framework could help change those incentives by rewarding genuine greenhouse gas reductions and creating a more level playing field”, says Fayas Malik Kanchiralla. Alternatives to adopting the Net-Zero Framework in full would be to remove certain elements of the climate regulations and agree on a modified version. However, the new study in Nature Energy shows that the details of the policy design matter for reducing the climate impact from shipping. “If we only put a price on emissions from ships’ exhaust gases, there is a risk on adoption of fuels that appear cleaner during use, but generate substantial greenhouse gas emissions during production. Our research shows why we need to consider the entire life cycle of marine fuels. Otherwise, a policy intended to reduce emissions could shift them upstream and, in some scenarios, increase the overall life-cycle climate impact,” says Fayas Malik Kanchiralla. articles.body: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price jumps as Singapore’s slides in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Europe Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has jumped $104/mt in the past week to $865/mt, while the Dutch port’s conventional VLSFO price has gained only $5/mt to $726/mt. This has widened Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $99/mt to $139/mt. Dutch suppliers can generate ZRE A tickets for selling low-carbon fuels, which can be traded with other suppliers. The price of these tickets has dropped from €215/mtCO2e ($241/mtCO2e) last Thursday to €197.5/mtCO2e ($219/mtCO2e) this week. These ZRE A tickets help lower Rotterdam’s biofuel prices compared with other ports. Belgium has no such mechanism. Lower ZRE A ticket prices could have supported Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price. This is despite indications of slightly lower feedstock costs. Prima Markets’ ARA UCOME and POMEME barge prices, both indicators of feedstock sourcing costs, have each dropped $8/mt in the past week, to $1,683/mt and $1,753/mt respectively. That leaves UCOME at a $70/mt discount to POMEME. Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO (POMEME) price has slipped $6/mt to $1,284/mt, while the port’s conventional LSMGO price has dropped a steeper $86/mt to $1,266/mt. This has flipped the blend from a $62/mt discount to conventional LSMGO last week to an $18/mt premium. B100 has been priced at $1,172/mt in Rotterdam today, up $9/mt on the week. In neighbouring Antwerp, B100 (UCOME) has been priced at $1,932/mt today, down $25/mt on the week. This puts it at a $760/mt premium over Rotterdam. Gibraltar’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) has been priced at $1,037/mt, a $210/mt premium over the port’s conventional VLSFO price of $827/mt. Asia Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has dropped $96/mt in the past week to $974/mt, while the port’s conventional VLSFO price has gained $5/mt to $852/mt. This has narrowed Singapore’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $101/mt to $122/mt. B100 has been priced at $1,374/mt in Singapore today, up $25/mt on the week. This has narrowed its premium over conventional VLSFO by $37/mt to $119/mt. That puts Hong Kong’s B30-VLSFO at a $26/mt premium over Singapore’s B30-VLSFO. If the framework is adopted, marine biodiesel use could rise to more than 12 billion litres/year (more than 10.68 million mt/year) by 2031. articles.body: Adani Ports taps more global lenders for $2.9-billion Evos acquisition funding in Port News 16/11/2026 Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone is looking to bring UAE’s First Abu Dhabi Bank and Singapore’s DBS Bank into the financing of its proposed acquisition of European liquid-storage operator Evos, widening the lender group beyond Japan’s MUFG, which has underwritten the transaction, people aware of the development told Moneycontrol.The company is discussing a mix of debt and its own equity contribution for the acquisition, which values Evos at €2.6 billion, or about $2.9 billion. Borrowings could account for half or more of the funding, with the eventual mix depending on how much cash Adani Ports chooses to deploy, the sources said. The discussions would broaden participation in a transaction for which financing commitments are already in place. MUFG is the sole underwriter and has committed up to €2.8 billion, Adani Ports said in its November 5 announcement. The equity contribution under consideration would allow Adani Ports to use its cash generation alongside bank funding. The company reported a cash balance of Rs 12,502 crore as of September 30. Indian public-sector banks have also been considered, although their participation appears less likely under the plan being discussed, the sources said. Evos operates liquid-storage terminals in Europe, earning fees for storing, handling and blending fuels and chemicals for energy companies, industrial customers and commodity traders. Emails sent to Adani group and DBS did not elicit a response till the time of publication. “As a matter of policy, FAB does not comment on individual client relationships, transactions, or market speculation. We remain committed to supporting our clients across the markets in which we operate and conducting our business in accordance with the highest standards of governance and regulatory compliance,” a spokesperson for First Abu Dhabi bank said in an email response. Adani Ports has agreed to acquire 100 percent of Netherlands-headquartered Evos from Igneo Infrastructure Partners. The transaction has an equity value of €1.18 billion and an enterprise value of €2.56-billion, which includes Evos’ debt. On an analyst call following the acquisition announcement, Adani Ports chief executive Ashwani Gupta said the combined business’s net debt-to-EBITDA ratio would be 2.76 times, before returning to the company’s guidance of 2.5 times by the end of FY27.The European purchase follows Adani Ports’ unsuccessful pursuit of Associated British Ports (ABP). An IFM Investors-managed fund agreed in October to acquire a 63.9 percent stake in the British operator at a reported valuation of about £10 billion. The parties did not disclose financial terms. ABP’s 2025 EBITDA of £473.7 million implies a multiple of roughly 21 times. On the other hand Evos is being acquired at 11.7 times its 2025 EBITDA, a substantially lower entry multiple, although the businesses differ in their asset mix and growth prospects. articles.summary: Asia is poised to enter Nov. 16 the January trading cycle for the spot LNG market, as the EU’s ban on Russian LNG from 2027 is expected to impact supply dynamics, though regional demand is anticipated to ultimately determine trade flows, market sources told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy.
