articles.body: EU’s Russia LNG ban from January to impact Asian supply; demand holds key in Freight News 16/11/2026 Asia is poised to enter Nov. 16 the January trading cycle for the spot LNG market, as the EU’s ban on Russian LNG from 2027 is expected to impact supply dynamics, though regional demand is anticipated to ultimately determine trade flows, market sources told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. The EU said it remains fully committed to implementing its planned ban on Russian natural gas and LNG imports to fully phase in over 2027. The EU is set to ban all imports of Russian LNG from Jan. 1, 2027, under legislation approved at the start of this year. Some European companies with long-term Russian LNG contracts can continue to divert shipments outside the EU until at least late July 2027 under a carve-out in the EU’s latest sanctions package against Moscow, approved in July. “It would be a strategic mistake to go back to an unreliable supplier that is waging an illegal war against Ukraine,” a European Commission spokesperson told Platts. “The RepowerEU gas regulation is in force and being implemented by the Member States. Pipeline gas and LNG imports [from Russia] are down from 45% in 2022 to just above 10% now. The deadline for last pipeline gas imports [from Russia] under long-term contracts is September 2027,” the EC spokesperson said. The realignment of Russian LNG flows is a long-pending outcome of the war in Europe that market mechanisms have been preparing for, Eric Yep, senior principal analyst for First Take Gas at S&P Global Energy CERA, said. “It will test many things, including current sanctions frameworks, the logistical ingenuity of Yamal LNG’s fleet, the risk appetite of Asian buyers and Russia’s political leverage to export its hydrocarbon,” Yep said. The EU’s ban on imports of Russian LNG is one of the key factors affecting the Asian LNG market after the January trading cycle, Asian market sources said. “If Europe increases its purchases of non-Russian LNG to replace Russian LNG, competition between Europe and Asia for flexible cargoes is likely to intensify. This could place upward pressure on spot supply-demand conditions and prices in Asia,” an Asian market source said. The JKM-TTF spread widened to 51.1 cents/MMBtu Nov. 12 after first narrowing to 39 cents/MMBtu Nov. 10, according to Platts data. However, the move was still insufficient to attract marginal LNG cargoes to Asia, with traders citing limited demand in the Japan-South Korea-Taiwan-China hub and stronger demand from Europe. “The arbitrage to send cargoes to Asia from West Africa and the US is shut at the moment. Europe will need to keep pulling marginal cargoes this winter,” a Singapore-based source said. Platts assessed the arbitrage to send cargoes to north Asia from West Africa and the US Gulf Coast via the Cape of Good Hope as closed at minus 0.2 cent/MMBtu and minus 88.2 cents/MMBtu, respectively, Nov. 12, after accounting for two-stroke vessel freight costs and carbon charges, favoring delivery to the Atlantic basin. However, the JKM-TTF spread could widen as the JKM pricing period rolls into January, potentially allowing marginal cargoes to flow to Asia amid uncertainty over weather and the potential for cold spells in Northeast Asia, an Atlantic-based source said. “The December-January structure could change. January is the peak peak,” the same source added. If Russian LNG that had been destined for the EU is redirected to third-country markets such as China, this could ease demand for non-Russian cargoes in Asia to some extent, the Asian market source said. “However, particularly for shipments from the Russian Arctic to Asia, there are constraints related to vessel availability and shipping routes,” the source said, adding that it would be difficult for all of the volumes previously destined for Europe to be redirected to Asia in the short term. Yamal LNG The impact of the EU’s ban is primarily centered around Russia’s Yamal LNG flows for winter, as Yamal exports to Europe have been strong due to trade flow restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, CERA’s Yep said. “However, this trade flow is expected to see a fundamental shift as the majority of Yamal LNG volumes that average around 20 million mt/year of LNG are redirected to Asia after Jan. 1,” Yep said. “This substantial volume needs to find alternative markets and will trigger a major shift in trade flows — Europe will need to attract a higher share of flexible supply and Yamal LNG will have to find a home in markets like China,” he said. A Singapore-based trader said Russian LNG cargoes will flow to Asia after January, but the supply may decline as Yamal LNG cargoes cannot be transported via the Northern Sea Route during winter. “Yamal volumes are entering China. Several Chinese companies have already secured Yamal cargoes on a spot basis and are marketing these volumes downstream for delivery early next year. We are still discussing a long-term contract with them,” said a source with a China-based company. Demand key Despite the EU ban on Russian LNG imports, market sources in Asia said winter and actual demand situations determine actual trading flows after January. “Assessing the actual impact will require a comprehensive examination of factors including temperatures in Europe and Northeast Asia, European gas storage levels, supply conditions from the Middle East and North America, and the extent to which Russian LNG is redirected to third-country markets,” said the Asian market source. EU-wide gas storage was 71.25% full as of Nov. 12, according to the latest data from Gas Infrastructure Europe. Asked about the impact of its Russian LNG import ban on European gas and LNG requirements for this winter, the EC spokesperson said, “Security of supply in the EU remains stable. Our main concern is the currently very high prices due to geopolitical events.” “We keep monitoring the situation very closely, but we are confident that we are well placed.” “There is less gas demand and more import flexibility than 5 years ago. And our infrastructure is resilient enough to increase LNG imports and meet winter demand,” the spokesperson said. “To ensure we are better prepared for future challenges, we are revising the EU energy security framework covering oil, gas and electricity based on lessons learned from the current and past crisis. These proposals are foreseen to be adopted in December,” the spokesperson added. The El Niño weather pattern is expected to reach its peak by the first half of winter and continue through spring 2027 with a 100% probability, the Japan Meteorological Agency said Nov. 10 in its latest monitoring and outlook. The El Niño has been watched as among the market-moving factors for this winter, as it typically results in warmer-than-usual weather in Japan and other parts of Asia. JFE is already involved through a separate contract to manufacture and transport monopile foundations at its Kasaoka facility. Akita Maritime Service will handle onshore transmission line inspections and arrange workboats and guard vessels. JFE currently provides maintenance services at Japan’s Nyuzen offshore wind farm, where it also operates its ASUNAG remote monitoring system. The Akita development was approximately 40% complete in November, with offshore turbine construction scheduled to begin during Japan’s 2027 financial year. articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy November 16, 2026 · 1 minute ago CETO wave energy unit makes a splash at BiMEP NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Carnegie Clean Energy Carnegie Clean Energy has deployed CETO wave energy system's buoyant actuator, the unit's prime mover, at the Biscay Marine Energy Platform (BiMEP) in Spain, as part of the first offshore deployment stage delivered in the ACHIEVE Programme. This initial short campaign aims to validate port and maritime authorization pathways, local supply chain logistics, quayside assembly, towing, and offshore installation operations and will deliver learnings for the next stage of deployment where the full CETO system will be deployed, including grid connection, planned for spring. The CETO buoyant actuator will remain at the offshore site at BiMEP in the Basque Country for a short period before being retrieved and brought back to port at the end of the current weather window. The completion of these activities is also said to unlock key funding milestones and financial support under the ACHIEVE Programme’s funding framework. "Seeing the CETO BA in the water offshore at the BiMEP site is a proud moment for everyone at Carnegie. It has taken a mammoth effort from our team in Bilbao to ensure the Stage 1 deployment has been a success," said Carnegie Chief Executive Officer, Jonathan Fiévez . "Whilst this is just the first stage of offshore campaign, the experience gained from this short deployment has increased our team’s capabilities and put us in a much stronger, more certain position as we push toward our full grid-connected Stage 2 deployment in European spring 2027. This is an ambitious project given the large technology leaps we’re taking so executing it in stages and conducting substantial onshore testing are important to manage risk.” Before deployment, the three modular sections of the buoyant actuator were transported from the local Basque fabricator to the Port of Bilbao, where they were assembled quayside. The buoyant actuator was then lowered by crane into the water and docked alongside the quay ready for transport to site. On November 14, the buoyant actuator was towed from the port to Carnegie’s pre-permitted offshore berth at BiMEP, where it was connected to a bespoke installed mooring and anchor system. Over the winter months, the CETO buoyant actuator will be kept onshore in the port while the power take-off (PTO) modules undergo final onshore testing locally, which includes a series of tests with the PTO modules and the electrical module simulating real ocean conditions to validate mechanical, electrical, control and communications functions. The transaction aims to strengthen international freight forwarding operations and expand logistics services across Southeast Asia. The agreement involves SCGJWD Freight (SJWDF), a...
articles.body: Thailand-based SCGJWD Logistics plans to acquire a stake of up to 24.5% in Triple i Logistics through a proposed business combination. The transaction aims to strengthen international freight forwarding operations and expand logistics services across Southeast Asia. The agreement involves SCGJWD Freight (SJWDF), a subsidiary of SCGJWD, and publicly listed Triple i Logistics. Under the proposed structure, SCGJWD will acquire newly issued Triple i shares through a share exchange and cash payment. It will also purchase existing shares from current shareholders. According to SCGJWD’s stock exchange filing, the total investment value will not exceed THB 1.62 billion. Following completion, SCGJWD is expected to hold up to 24.5% of Triple i. Meanwhile, the freight forwarding business currently operated by SJWDF will become part of Triple i through a corporate restructuring. The companies expect to complete the transaction during the first quarter of 2027. However, the agreement remains subject to approval by Triple i shareholders and other transaction conditions. Partnership to strengthen regional freight forwarding The proposed combination brings together the two companies’ different logistics capabilities. SCGJWD contributes sea freight operations, regional logistics infrastructure and an established customer network. Its activities also include warehousing, customs brokerage, cross-border transportation and distribution. Triple i, meanwhile, brings expertise in air freight forwarding and aviation-related logistics. The company also operates through an extensive network of domestic and international partners. By combining these operations, the companies aim to develop a broader freight forwarding platform covering sea, air and land transportation. The partnership is also expected to improve purchasing power, expand service coverage and create additional opportunities across their existing customer networks. “Strengthening our position in ASEAN requires more than expanding our geographical presence. It requires the ability to connect markets through a comprehensive logistics network and deliver integrated solutions that meet customers’ increasingly complex supply chain needs,” said Bunn Kasemsup, Co-CEO, SCGJWD. SCGJWD Logistics Co-CEOs: Mr. Bunn Kasemsup (L) and Mr. Charvanin Bunditkitsada (R) Transaction expected to close in early 2027 The planned integration comes as logistics providers seek greater flexibility in response to changing international trade conditions. SCGJWD said the combination would allow customers to access a wider range of transport options across Southeast Asia. These include international freight forwarding, cross-border road transport, warehousing and distribution. The company also highlighted the importance of alternative transport routes during periods of geopolitical disruption and changing trade restrictions. Following completion, both businesses are expected to continue serving customers under their existing brands. The freight forwarding operations of SJWDF will retain the SCGJWD identity while gaining access to Triple i’s broader service network. The transaction remains conditional, with the final ownership structure subject to completion of the planned share exchange, cash investment and corporate restructuring.

articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) has resumed transits through the Suez Canal, with the container ship ONE CONTINUITY passing through the waterway on 15 November 2026. The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) confirmed that the vessel crossed the canal as part of the southbound convoy during its voyage from Singapore to the Netherlands. The 8,110-TEU container ship measures 320 metres in length and 46 metres in width. It has a gross tonnage of approximately 88,000. ONE CONTINUITY operates on the FE1 service of the Premier Alliance, which comprises ONE, HMM and Yang Ming. The service connects major ports in the Far East with Northwest Europe. The transit marks another development in the gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal following widespread diversions around the Cape of Good Hope. Three more Premier Alliance services expected to return Suez Canal Authority Chairman Ossama Rabiee said three additional Premier Alliance services are scheduled to resume transits through the canal instead of sailing around the Cape of Good Hope. However, the authority did not identify the three services or provide a timetable for their return. Rabiee also stated that the Suez Canal is ready to operate at full capacity and accommodate the return of large container vessels. According to the SCA, the authority has maintained contact with shipping lines throughout the Red Sea crisis. These discussions have focused on geopolitical developments, market conditions and the gradual restoration of vessel traffic. The latest transit provides a further indication of changing routing patterns on the Asia–Europe trade. Nevertheless, a broader restoration of Premier Alliance services remains subject to the planned changes being implemented. Shorter route offers operational advantages Captain Oleksandr Shumakov, Master of ONE CONTINUITY, highlighted the operational advantages of using the Suez Canal for voyages between Asia and Europe. According to Shumakov, the shorter route can reduce sailing distances, improve cargo delivery times and lower fuel consumption compared with navigating around the Cape of Good Hope. He also praised the navigational services provided by the Suez Canal Authority, including the support of canal pilots and escort tugboats. The SCA has continued developing the waterway by extending sections with two-way navigation and widening parts of the channel. The return of ONE CONTINUITY comes as shipping lines reassess their routing strategies following prolonged disruption in the Red Sea region. Further changes across the Premier Alliance network could increase container vessel traffic through the Suez Canal if the planned service returns proceed.

The Naples-based company will see the 9,200 dwt unit delivered in July 2028, according to shipbroking sources, although the yard has not disclosed a delivery date or contract price. The order follows Ve-Na’s first contract with the Guangxi yard in May 2025. That earlier vessel has reached the quayside commissioning stage, with completion scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. The Italian owner specialises in general cargo shipping, with vessel databases identifying three existing ships in its fleet. The newbuilding adds to a growing portfolio of small and medium-sized merchant vessels being constructed by the Guangxi yard for European operators. The latest contract is the eighth 9,200 dwt general cargo vessel secured by CSSC Guangxi across its European customer base, although the yard has not disclosed how many of the series belong to Ve-Na. articles.body: Americas Contributions Operations Why a collision with no deaths got more attention than two wars at sea Splash November 16, 2026 0 493 3 minutes read U.S. Coast Guard Heartland U.S. Coast Guard Heartland Dustin Eno, a crisis communications consultant, and founder of the Maritime Attention Index, gives his take on Friday’s high-profile allision in New Orleans. On Friday November 13, Iran said an LNG tanker had hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz and exploded. That afternoon in New Orleans, the tanker Atlantic Asphalt ran into the river cruise ship American Heritage at her berth on the Mississippi and capsized her. One of those stories sent the Maritime Attention Index , which I edit, from 91 to 188 over the weekend, its highest reading since June. And it wasn’t the story with a global impact. The incident in New Orleans was serious and could have been much worse. Nearly 200 people were aboard the American Heritage , passengers ended up in the river and more than 30 were taken to hospital. But nobody died, there was no pollution, and the knock-on effects will be fairly minor. Compare that with the two wars being fought at sea. The UN counts 25 seafarers killed in and around Hormuz since the war with Iran began, oil from attacked tankers has closed beaches in the UAE, and the knock-on effects have global significance. In the Black Sea, drones have sunk cargo ships off Romania and Bulgaria, and the Financial Times now calls it the world’s deadliest shipping route. The insurance losses from either war dwarf anything the Mississippi will produce. By almost any measure of harm, the wars are the bigger story. Popular wisdom, as encapsulated by the old newsroom maxim, “If it bleeds, it leads”, is that the most destructive events will get the most attention. So why did the wars lose the attention battle this weekend? Four reasons Everyone saw the cruise ship capsize. The allision (collision with a stationary object) was filmed by several people, from several angles, at every stage — the tanker coming in, the impact, the riverboat going over, passengers swimming to safety. An attack in the Gulf or the Black Sea usually reaches us as a statement from a navy or a ministry, perhaps with a photo of smoke on the horizon taken hours later. It happened in America. New Orleans sits inside the biggest news market in the world, with crews minutes from the riverbank. The Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea are over the horizon for most of the outlets that set the global agenda, and the ships attacked there rarely belong to anyone their readers have heard of. It had passengers. Passengers are people the audience can imagine being. Seafarers, however much the industry talks about them, are not. In the same week that the Philippines announced all 17 Filipino crew on the Atlantic Asphalt were safe, it was bringing home the body of a Filipino seafarer killed in a drone strike in the Gulf. I suspect few readers outside the Philippines saw the second story. Novelty did the rest. If a tanker had hit a passenger ship every week since July, Friday’s allision would not have caused the index to spike. That is what has happened to both wars. An attack on a container ship off Oman in late July took the index to 165. When tankers were hit in Hormuz at the start of this month, it stayed below 80, and a drone sinking a cargo ship off Romania in October barely moved it. The attacks have not stopped — we have got used to them. The spike could have been bigger still. The same evening, the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop, and American newsrooms spent part of Friday night splitting their airtime between a capsized riverboat and grounded flights. Who’s the tanker owner? There is one name you will have struggled to find in any of the mainstream coverage — the company behind the Atlantic Asphalt . Most reports refer only to “the tanker’s owners”, and mostly because the Port of New Orleans is now suing them for more than $1m. The voices of this story have been the Coast Guard, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the port. That is a fairly classic pattern for an incident in the US. The coverage is enormous, but the authorities communicate early and well, and they take the questions. That takes pressure off the shipping company, but it can also leave it with very little say in how the story is told. So far, that has probably worked out fine. The headline everyone is using is “miracle on the Mississippi”, and the official explanation is that the tanker lost control. But the authorities’ job is to explain the response, not to speak for the ship. When the investigation turns to why she lost control, the company may find the story has already been written by others.
